newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma blames bomb attack on exiles, rebels.
newsitem.headline: Burma blames bomb attack on exiles, rebels.

text.p: Burma's military government blamed exiled students and the rebel Karen National Union (KNU) on Friday for the Christmas Day bomb attack at a religious site which killed five people and wounded 17.
The death toll rose to five from four after one of the wounded died from injuries sustained in Wednesday's blast at the Buddhist Maha Pasana Cave.

Thousands of pilgrims were paying homage to the famous Lord Buddha's Sacred Tooth Relic on display at the site when two bombs went off at different places. All the dead and wounded were from the second bomb.
The relic was on loan from China.

"According to intelligence reports, the All-Burma Students Democratic Front (ABSDF) and the Karen National Union have concocted a plan to destabilise the peaceful situation prevailing in the country by terrorist activities," a government statement said.

"It is also learnt that these terrorists had also intended to destroy the Sacred Tooth Relic with the intent to create a diplomatic row between the People's Republic of China and the Union of Myanmar (Burma)," it added.
"In this regard, explosives training courses have been given by certain foreign elements to the KNU and ABSDF insurgents," the statement said.
The Chinese Embassy in Rangoon denounced the bomb attack on Thursday.
"The bomb attacks ... blaspheme the Buddha and go against the will of the people," the embassy said in a statement.
The Sacred Tooth Relic, believed to be a tooth of the Lord Buddha, arrived in Burma on December 6 on loan for 90 days. It was not damaged, media reported on Thursday.
Public access to the relic, suspended on Thursday after the blasts, resumed on Friday. Access was limited to between 6 a.m. and 5 p.m. daily and not 24 hours as before.
Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), which took power in 1988, faced renewed unrest in the past month when students staged two weeks of street protests.
It also faces rebel ethnic guerrilla armies such as the KNU in eastern Burma.

Neighbouring China is one of a handful of countries to maintain close ties with the SLORC, which has been accused by Western nations of widespread human rights abuses, including restrictions on Nobel Peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi.
Suu Kyi heads the opposition National League for Democracy.
In another preventive measure, the SLORC said it had postponed indefinitely the Seventh Mayor's International Marathon, which was scheduled to be held in Rangoon on December 30.

The marathon, in which about 50,000 international runners usually compete, was originally due to be held on December 14. But it was postponed to December 30 because of anti-government student unrests earlier this month.
Official media hit out at those responsible for the bomb attack and urged the Burmese people to be vigilant against destructive groups.

"We must keep our eyes and ears alert and keep vigil with security awareness against the danger of destructive elements' brazen perpetrations and endeavour to expose them before they could strike again," one newspaper editorial said.
